en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Seven:
Clarifying the Ten Stages, divided into ten sections. First: The Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
"Ānanda! This son of good family has attained excellent penetration into Great Bodhi; his awakening penetrates suchness..."
"Come, that which exhausts the realm of the Buddha is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Bodhi is the awakening of a Buddha.
The former is like having emerged but not yet fully emerged, like the precursor of fire, which is termed 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*)."
Now, just as when fire emerges, the wood is exhausted and the ashes fly away while the smoke is extinguished, it is therefore said that one has attained excellent penetration.
Thus, this first stage is called the Stage of Penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), for the principle of the Buddha’s entire realm is fully revealed.

Because one has attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and thoroughly realized that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the single, true equality, free from the characteristics of subject and object; as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When, with respect to the object of cognition, the wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because one is free from the characteristics of the two grasps."

It further states: "One thoroughly masters the dharma-realm and attains the equality of the single truth; even reaching the universal true thusness (sarvatraga-tathatā), one leaves behind the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-dhātu-āvaraṇa) and excels in the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā)."

Regarding the term "pervasive practice" (*vyāpaka-caryā*): because this *tathatā* (suchness) pervades all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) and has now been realized, whereby one attains mastery in benefiting oneself and others, it is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The *Avataṃsaka* and the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Renwang) explain its characteristics in detail; they are not recorded here in full, and all subsequent sections follow this pattern.
2. The Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
"Different natures enter into sameness, and those of the same nature are also extinguished; this is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.

In the preceding ground, one has skillfully attained thorough penetration into Great Bodhi, departed from worldly characteristics, entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), destroyed the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), and realized the single true Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that "different natures enter into sameness."
In this stage, even the identity of differences cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is said that "the same nature is also extinguished.
If one perceives identity, it is termed a defilement.
Since all oppositions have been transcended, it is called "free from defilement" (vimalā).

Furthermore, this stage realizes the most excellent *tathatā* (suchness) and is free from the obstacles of improper conduct; because the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is preeminent there, and it is manifested through natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*), it is called "most excellent."

By practicing the ten wholesome paths of action on a vast scale through the four immeasurable minds, one attains the accomplishment of natural precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*). Regarding both the naturally grave offenses and those involving social censure, one regards them with equal impartiality without distinction; this is also called "entering sameness despite differing natures.

When even the notion of a "nature" is severed, one is finally freed from the defilement of subtle violations of the precepts; this is called "the extinction of the same nature," and the stage is thus named the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Third, the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*).
"When purity reaches its ultimate limit, brilliance arises; this is named the Ground of Radiant Light.

Because one achieves supreme meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇīs, and because transgressions of the precepts and afflictions (*kleśa*) ultimately do not arise, it is called "purity reaching its ultimate limit."
Because it can emit the boundless light of wondrous wisdom, it is called "the arising of illumination.

On this stage, one realizes the "superior-flowing *tathatā*," meaning that the teaching flowing from this *tathatā* is the most excellent among all other teachings; thus, one abandons the obstacle of dullness and darkness, and the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) becomes increasingly superior.
Fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*):
"When clear illumination reaches its ultimate fulfillment, it is called the Ground of Blazing Wisdom.
Because wisdom is generated from meditative concentration and the light of that wisdom is vast and serene, it is said to be the "ultimate fulfillment of clear illumination."
Because it can destroy the subtle afflictive hindrances until they are exhausted, it is called "Perfection of Enlightenment" (*bodhimāna*).
Because the flames of enlightenment have increased, it is called "Blazing Wisdom" (*jvālāprajñā*).

On this stage, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) of non-appropriation; that is to say, because this *tathatā* is never again grasped by the self-clinging of the sixth consciousness—due to the permanent severance of the two types of view of a self-body—it is able to eliminate the hindrance of the manifestation of subtle afflictions, and the cultivation of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) becomes preeminent.
5. The Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
"That which cannot be reached by anything either identical or different is called the Ground of Difficult to Conquer.
Because true wisdom is unique, it is said to be "identical"; [yet it is not reached by that which is different].
Because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) involves differentiation, it is said to be "different.

Since the modes of activity of true and conventional wisdom are mutually contradictory, to bring them into union and accord is to be neither identical nor different; therefore, it is said that [this state] is "that which cannot be reached."
It is exceedingly sublime and unsurpassed by anything else; therefore, it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya).

On this stage, one realizes the Suchness of Non-differentiation of Categories (*jāty-aviśeṣa-tathatā*); that is to say, this Suchness does not possess distinct categories like those of the eye and other sense organs. One abandons the obstacles to the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle and cultivates the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) with increasing excellence.
Sixth, the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
"The unconditioned nature of *tathatā* is pure and luminously revealed; this is called the Ground of Manifestation.
This means that by abiding in the wisdom of dependent origination, one draws forth the most excellent non-conceptual *prajñā*, causing it to become manifest before one.
Because wisdom is manifest and principle is manifest, it is said that the unconditioned nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is pure and luminously revealed.

On this stage, one realizes the undefiled and pure true suchness; that is to say, this true suchness is by nature undefiled, and it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later. Thus, one severs the obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse characteristics and cultivates the *prajñāpāramitā* with increasing excellence.
7. The Ground of Far-Going (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
"Reaching the limit of the ultimate reality (*tathatā*) is called the Ground of Far-Going.
Because one attains the mind of the single *tathatā* in the eighth ground, it is named "signless" (*animitta*) and "effortless" (*anābhoga*).

Therefore, from the initial generation of the mind in this seventh stage, throughout two incalculable eons, one applies effort and practice; now, having reached the final limit of effort characterized by signs, and because one has transcended the paths of the world and the two vehicles, one arrives at the ultimate boundary of signless *tathatā*. Hence, it is said that "one exhausts the limit of *tathatā*."
Because one has practiced for many eons, it is called "Far-reaching.

One realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) that is undifferentiated among all phenomena; this means that although this suchness is established in various ways through numerous teachings, it remains without distinction.
The obstacle to the manifestation of subtle characteristics is severed, and the practice of skillful means becomes increasingly superior.
Eighth is the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
"The mind of true suchness is called the Immovable Ground."

Because it is neither defiled nor pure, it is called "one"; because it is free from all falsehoods, it is called "true"; because it is eternally abiding and unchanging, it is called "thusness" (tathatā); and with reference to this meaning, it is called "immovable."

Furthermore, because non-conceptual wisdom flows on spontaneously and continuously within this stage, and it cannot be disturbed by signs, functions, or afflictions, it is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

On this stage, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is neither increasing nor decreasing; that is to say, this *tathatā* is free from the grasping at increase or decrease, as it does not undergo increase or decrease according to defilement or purity. One abandons the obstacle to applying effort toward signlessness and cultivates the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) with increased excellence.
9. The Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
"The manifestation of the function of *tathatā* is called the Ground of Excellent Intelligence.

Based on the essence of the principle of *tathatā*, one gives rise to the function of unimpeded wisdom, accomplishing the four subtle and wondrous analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and being able to skillfully preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions; therefore, it is named the Ground of Excellent Intelligence.

On this stage, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) of mastery over knowledge; that is to say, once this *tathatā* has been realized, one attains mastery over the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), namely: dharma, meaning, expression, and eloquence.

This means that these four kinds have wisdom as their essence and are called "mastery over wisdom"; they sever the obstacle of lack of desire for practice within the gateway of benefiting others, and they consist in the predominance of the cultivation of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
10. The Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), in two parts:
first, the introduction. "Ānanda!..."
"From this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and bring their merit to perfection; thus, this stage is also called the 'Stage of Cultivation' (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).

This refers to the period from the second stage (*dvitīyā-bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), as these constitute the fourth among the five stages; alternatively, it may refer collectively to all fifty-five stages from the preceding [first stage] up to this point.
This tenth stage is the ultimate limit of cultivation; thus, this stage is also named the "Stage of Cultivation.
Second, the explicit manifestation:
"The wondrous cloud of the canopy of loving-kindness covers the ocean of nirvāṇa; it is called the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*)."
The essence of bodhicitta does not depart from two aspects, namely compassion and wisdom.
From its initial cultivation until the completion of its task, these are fused into the ocean of fruition, which is called the Dharmakāya.
Compassion (*maitrī*) is itself pity (*karuṇā*); because it can provide shade for sentient beings, it is called the "compassionate canopy.
The "wondrous cloud" is wisdom (*jñāna*), and *nirvāṇa* is the principle (*tattva*).
The *dharmakāya* is without marks; these three alone are also termed the great samādhi, wisdom, and compassion—namely, the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*, known as the "Secret Treasury."

In this present stage, one still dwells at the ultimate limit of cultivation; yet, obstacles to the Buddha-ground still remain, such that the initial awakening has not yet merged with the fundamental [awakening], and the two marks still persist. Therefore, it is said that the ocean of nirvāṇa is covered.
This stage is the basis for realizing the *tathatā* (suchness) of mastery over karma; that is to say, once this *tathatā* has been realized, one attains four kinds of mastery:

first, mastery over the three types of action; second, mastery over the five supernormal powers; third, mastery over *dhāraṇī*; and fourth, mastery over meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). By severing the obstacles to mastery regarding all phenomena, one cultivates the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) with increasing excellence.
8. The Stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi): two parts.
First, the direct explanation:

"The Tathāgata flows against the current; likewise, the Bodhisattva proceeds in accordance with it until they reach the point where the limits of awakening intersect—this is called Equal Enlightenment."

Arising from the Truth to manifest in response, returning to the cycle of birth and death, and beginning the process of entering from the fruit back into the cause—this is why it is said that the Tathāgata flows against the current.
The noble wisdom of the fruit-dharma is itself the flow of the Dharma.
From cause one enters the fruit; from birth-and-death one enters nirvana. Therefore, it is called "reaching through following the course.
"Reaching" (zhì) means the ultimate limit.

It is the beginning of the arising of response and the culmination of practicing the causes; the intersection of the forward and reverse movements occurs in a single kṣaṇa. Hence, it is said: "Awakening at the limit, entering the intersection."

This is precisely the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) preceding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); it is at this very stage that one is established as an Equal Awakened One (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).

Although the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* does not explicitly state this, it is implicitly contained within the tenth stage; therefore, the attainment of office (*abhiṣeka*) within that stage is explained as being the state of Equal Awakening.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* merely refutes eleven kinds of obstacles; this is precisely that same intent.
That it is presented separately here is intended to fully manifest the sequential progression (*xingbu*) within the context of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
2. Conclusion and Manifestation.
"Ānanda! From the mind of dry wisdom up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, this awakening is first attained within the diamond-like mind."

Although from the initial resolve until this stage of Perfect Enlightenment one employs the Vajra-samādhi to observe that all phenomena are like illusions and so forth, yet upon reaching this stage, it is able to destroy the final subtle ignorance; as this is the ultimate limit of this samādhi and its power and function are fully perfected, it is specifically named the "Vajra-mind."

This is precisely the initial moment when wondrous enlightenment enters the mind; it belongs to the path of non-interruption (ānantarya-mārga) and is thus termed "Equal Enlightenment" (samyak-sambodhi). Therefore, it is said that one has "initially attained the Vajra-mind.
This is what the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains: "When the Vajra-like Samādhi manifests, one severs the obstacles of the Buddha-stage and immediately enters Wondrous Enlightenment."
9. The Stage of Sublime Enlightenment.

"From the initial Ground of Dry Wisdom, through these successive layers of single and double stages totaling twelve, one finally exhausts the state of Sublime Enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way."

"From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) at the beginning, up to the Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) at the end, there are twelve stages in total, comprising both single and combined categories.

There are seven single stages, namely: Dry Wisdom, Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), the World-High (*laukikāgra-dharma*), Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and Wondrous Enlightenment."

Furthermore, there are five [stages], namely: faith (*śraddhā*), abiding (*sthiti*), practice (*caryā*), orientation (*pratipatti*), and the ground (*bhūmi*). Because each individual stage itself possesses these ten [qualities], they are called "repeated" (*puṭa*).
The twelfth stage is that of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is named the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).

The Unsurpassed One is so called because there is nothing further to be severed; the Unsurpassed One is such that no one can surpass him. Just as the moon on the fifteenth day is perfectly full and without defect, it is said that only upon reaching this point does one exhaustively perfect wondrous enlightenment and achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
The essence is Great Parinirvāṇa; being fully endowed with the three virtues, it is called the Secret Treasury.
Third, the conclusion on the establishment of stages based on practice, in three parts:
first, the conclusion on the practice of function.

"These various stages are all realized through the diamond-like contemplation of the ten profound metaphors for illusoriness; within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of the Tathāgatas to purify, cultivate, and realize them, gradually entering ever deeper."
The phrase "various" refers to the preceding fifty-seven stages; thus it is said.

In each and every stage, one employs the Vajra-like Illusory Samādhi to observe all phenomena. Whether in terms of practice or wisdom, all that is severed and realized is like illusions, mirages, the moon in water, space, echoes, cities of Gandharvas, dreams, shadows, images, and transformations; hence they are called the "ten kinds of profound metaphors."

This means that from the initial gradual stages up to the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, all are achieved through the King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi—namely, the cessation inherent in contemplation and the contemplation inherent in cessation—which destroys the delusions of ignorance and gives rise to practice, cultivation, and realization; therefore, it is called "adamantine observation."
Vipaśyanā is the simultaneous integration of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Thus, Jingxi said:
"As one exerts oneself as if in a dream, the delusion of the name 'emptiness' ceases; once the causes of illusion are fulfilled, the fruit of the mirror-image is perfected."

Qingliang said: "One cultivates the myriad practices that are like flowers in the sky, sits peacefully in a meditation hall that is like the moon in water, subdues the celestial Māras who are like reflections in a mirror, and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream."
All of this is intended to convey this meaning.
Second, the conclusion of the sequence of stages: "Ānanda!..."
"In this way, by means of these three progressive advancements (*abhyudgama*), one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
"Progressive advancement" refers to gradual progression; therefore, the preceding text states: "From this point on, the holy stages are established gradually."
Regarding the fifty-five stages: faith, abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds constitute fifty; while dry wisdom, heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharma constitute five.
Bodhi is the fruit, namely the two types of awakening: the equal and the wondrous.
The fifty-five mental states are called the "path," for by means of them one can reach the fruit of bodhi; thus, they are the path to bodhi.
3. Conclusion on the Erroneous and the Correct:
"One who practices this contemplation is said to practice correctly; one who contemplates otherwise is said to contemplate erroneously.

If a practitioner can cultivate and realize according to this, attaining cessation through non-cessation and arrival through non-arrival, they are then called a true practitioner of cultivation; therefore, it is termed "correct contemplation."
If one claims that there are no stages at all and that merely adhering to principle is sufficient, this is identical to the false view that negates cause and effect;

therefore, it is called "erroneous contemplation. This is also discerned in the *Renwang jing*, which, after explaining the stages, states: "To say that one attains Buddhahood by transcending these [stages] is the teaching of Māra."

The fifth major section, "Distinguishing the Names of the Sacred Teachings," concludes the preceding texts, which have relied on understanding to give rise to practice; through the gradual stages of cultivation, the fruit is realized from the cause, completing the entire cycle of a single lifetime.
This Dharma-gate shall flow down to future generations; it is necessary to establish a title for the scripture. If its name did not exist, by what means could one summon its essence to circulate it?
Therefore, this text has come forth.
Part Two: I. Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What shall this sutra be named?
How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?

Mañjuśrī, whose wisdom and virtue were foremost in this assembly, was the first to ask; while Ānanda encountered the calamity of Laṅkā, the Buddha commanded him to go and rescue her by means of a dhāraṇī.
The great assembly was bewildered and lost their bearings, yet they also sought the source through further inquiry;
the various sages each spoke of their own perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), and the Tathāgata commanded them to select with care.
Now that my understanding and practice are perfected and the cycle of cause and effect is complete, I therefore inquire about the name of this sutra so that it may circulate for future generations.
First, the affairs of this assembly were entrusted to this person.
Second, the Tathāgata’s response:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"This sutra is titled 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Śītavana-Bhadrā Anuttara-Ratna-Mudrā, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions. The five names listed below are, for now, this one."
This is because the Buddha emits light from his invisible crown and manifests transformation Buddhas who preach divine mantras.
This represents the unity of the essence, characteristics, and functions of the One Mind.
"Great" (Mahā) refers to the essence;
The Buddha represents the *lakṣaṇa* (the marks);
the transformation Buddhas in the halo of light on the crown represent the *karman* (the function).

To explain this in detail according to the method of correspondence: regarding the title’s mention of *Sitatātapatra* and so forth, it is called the "White Parasol" (*Sitatātapatra*). The "white" signifies that the heart of the *dharmadhātu* is unstained; "parasol" signifies that it universally covers all things.

The wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the honored Dharma; it definitively distinguishes the correct from the erroneous, and only a Buddha-to-Buddha can exhaustively fathom it—this is called the Unsurpassed Treasure Seal.

All Buddhas of the three periods of time use this to illuminate the true mark of all phenomena; vertically penetrating the past and present and horizontally pervading all directions, it is endowed with untainted virtues and is called the Pure Ocean Eye.
The above is a general designation established based on both wisdom and principle.

Second: "It is also named 'Saving and Protecting the Immediate Cause, Delivering Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly by Nature, Causing Them to Attain Bodhicitta and Enter the Ocean of Universal Knowledge.'"
"Rescuing and protecting one's kinsmen" is the general heading;
"delivering and liberating [them]" below it is the specific exposition;
"attaining the bodhicitta" refers to generating the aspiration for the Mahāyāna.
"Entering the ocean of universal knowledge and realizing the principle of perfect permanence.
This above establishes the name based on its function and efficacy.
"It is also called 'The Definitive Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Practice, and Realization,'" which is the third.
The persons who have realized the fruits throughout the three periods of time enter the secret treasury by taking this as their cause;

thus, it is the "secret cause. Furthermore, because this Great Samādhi encompasses all practices yet cannot be known by ordinary or Hinayana practitioners, it is called "secret," and this "secret" is precisely the cause.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have taught this Dharma-gate as the ultimate discourse; therefore, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*).
This name is established in reference to both the person [the Buddha] and the Dharma.
"It is also named 'The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions,'" which is the fourth [title].

It is "Great" because its vastness encompasses the boundless; it is "Square" because the True Dharma maintains itself; it is "Broad" because it pervades everywhere in accordance with its essence—these are the meanings of the Three Greatnesses.

"Wondrous" refers to the inconceivable; the metaphor of the lotus flower signifies the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, for by emerging from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance of knowledge, one perceives the Buddha-nature, just as a flower emerges from the water and blooms.
Furthermore, because one attains mastery over the Dharma and is the foremost among all samādhis, it is called "King.
Because it gives birth to all Buddhas, it is called "Mother.
Because it maintains the good, wards off the evil, and universally encompasses all merits, it is called "Dhāraṇī."
"Mantra" (zhòu) is synonymous with "incantation" (zǔ).
This name is established based on its manifest benefits.
It is also called "The Mantras for Consecration," "The Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas," and "Śūraṅgama."
"You should uphold this.
This is the fifth [point].
Because it is the clear instruction by which the Dharma King entrusts his governance, it is called the "Mantra of Consecration" (Abhiṣeka-pada).
The various bodhisattvas have already been explained as above;
these names are established based on their teaching and practice.
The five names mentioned above answer the first question, while "you should uphold them" answers the second question.

Simply relying on the preceding five names, one acts according to what has been taught; by transmitting this to future generations so that the multitude may attain awakening, one is truly upholding [the teaching].
The above clarifies understanding and discerning practice, wherein the cause leads to the fruit, thereby revealing the distinctions between the stages.

When the request for the names [of the recipients] has been made and the single session has concluded, this marks the end of the assembly; it should be stated that the great multitude, having heard what the Buddha taught, prostrated and departed.
Ānanda requested further instruction once more; although time had elapsed between these occasions, his inquiries were continuous.
Therefore, the compilers of the scriptures, grouping the questions according to their meaning, combined them into a single section.
For this reason, they did not take their leave by bowing, but departed as they were.
Section Six, the Great Text, which distinguishes the differences in the causes for rebirth in various destinies: from this point onward is the second assembly’s reiteration of the sutra.

Because Ānanda’s questions regarding the phenomena he had witnessed differed [from what was previously taught], this has already been explained according to the sequence of the teachings—beginning, middle, and end.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, Ānanda’s question, which is further divided into two.
I. Narrating the Attainment of the Fruit, in two parts:
1. The Increase of the Path through Hearing the Dharma.

Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the *Guhyamudrā-pāṭala*, as well as the definitive names and titles of this sutra. They suddenly awakened to the profound principle of the progressive advancement through the noble stages of *dhyāna*. Their minds became tranquil and concentrated, severing the six grades of subtle afflictions that must be cultivated away within the three realms.
Having attained true samādhi, it is called "sudden enlightenment in dhyāna.
Having realized the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, it is called "cultivating progress toward the noble stages.
Having profoundly verified the Truth of Cessation, it is called "the supreme, wondrous principle."
As wisdom gradually becomes clear and its illumination expands, it is said that "the mind and its deliberations are empty and stilled.
Because that which is innate is difficult to eliminate, it is termed "subtle.

Regarding the mention of "six grades," according to the Mahāyāna teaching, although the innate afflictions (*kleśa*) in each of the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms are each divided into nine grades, for those whose wisdom increases, these are permanently suppressed upon entering the stages and are only severed upon reaching Buddhahood.
If compassion increases, one intentionally brings it forth.

If following the Hīnayāna, each of the nine stages is likewise divided into nine grades; however, since the abandonment occurs separately at each stage according to the four fruits of the path, one realizes the second fruit by abandoning the first six grades of afflictions within the single stage of the desire realm while still in the body of the first fruit;
and one realizes the third fruit by abandoning the lower three grades while in the body of the second fruit.
Within the body of the third fruit, one abandons seventy-two grades of afflictions of the two upper realms and immediately attains arhatship.
Since he has now realized the second fruit, he has abandoned six grades.
Second, praising the Buddha and describing the benefits.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, whose compassionate voice is all-encompassing, you have skillfully opened up the subtle and deep-seated delusions of sentient beings, causing my body and mind today to feel such joy and granting me great benefit.”
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*) are difficult to discern; therefore, they are called "subtle.
Being co-emergent from beginningless time, they are called "deep-seated delusions.
Because the net of doubt has been eliminated, it is said to be "refreshing."
Because it advances one toward the noble stages (*ārya-pada*), it is called "beneficial" (*anugraha*).
Second, the statement of the doubts, which has two parts:
first, the formal presentation of the questions; second, [the actual questions]. (The second part follows.)
First, a general inquiry regarding the various realms of existence:
"World-Honored One!

If this wondrously bright, truly pure, and sublime mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect, such that even the great earth, grasses, trees, and wriggling sentient beings are fundamentally True Suchness (Tathatā), then they are the true essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood."
The Buddha-body is the ultimate reality; how then can there still be the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas?
World-Honored One!
"Does this path exist inherently from the beginning,
or does it arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings?
This doubt arises because of the previous words of the Buddha to Ānanda:

"Now that your sense faculties have been completely uprooted and their inner luminosity has begun to radiate, you—along with these ephemeral phenomena and the various transformations of the vessel-world—will, like ice melting in hot water, be transformed in an instant into supreme awareness."
"In this case, when one person attains Buddhahood, the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) and its sentient beings (*sattva*) would all attain Buddhahood simultaneously.

Since the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood long ago today, it would be illogical for there to still exist a vessel-world or various realms of rebirth; therefore, it is asked: 'How can the true body of the Buddha still have paths such as the hells?'"

If this Way were inherently present from the beginning, why did you previously state that it is "pure and fundamental by nature" and that "from the beginning there have been no worlds or sentient beings"?
Furthermore, one could not say that when a single person attains Buddhahood, the primary and secondary realms merge into awakening.
If it is said that sentient beings arise from the habituation of delusion, how does this habituation of delusion come to arise?
What is the meaning of the characteristics of such arising?

According to the intent of the Tathāgata’s response, it is that sentient beings create karma through delusion and undergo birth through delusion; within the mind of Bodhi, these are like flowers in the sky—delusory perceptions of arising and ceasing.
Therefore, the subsequent text says: "You have created this falsely for yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi.
Question: How does this differ from the doubts held by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra?
Answer: The former doubt was that the fundamental principle is inherently pure; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
This takes the "retributive environment" as the primary focus to challenge the notion of inherent purity.

Therefore, the Buddha explained away these doubts: it is because of forceful awakening that one falsely discriminates between subject and object, thereby giving rise to the three kinds of continuity. These arise from deluded vision; thus, due to this unreality, they end only to begin again.

This doubt arises from the thought that now that the Buddha has attained fruition, all things have merged and returned to awakening; how then can there still be distinctions among the seven destinies?

This objection takes the primary retribution as its starting point, challenging that the Buddha of fruition is solely the Truth, and that within the Truth there cannot exist these seven kinds of disparity.
Furthermore, one might inquire: does this path exist inherently, or does it arise falsely?

The intention is for the Tathāgata to explain extensively that although both cause and effect are ultimately illusory, the karmic conditions of good and evil and the resulting retributions—whether favorable or unfavorable—are never subject to error; thus, he shall cause all sentient beings to clearly understand cause and effect and not fall into false views.
The preceding text merely stated that "it arises from deluded vision and is of one essence with falsehood.
Those of dull faculties might then conclude that cause and effect are entirely non-existent.

Now, through this analysis, cause and effect are made manifest; thus we know that the intent of the previous objection was to reveal the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), while the intent of the present doubt is to clarify conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Only when the preceding and succeeding parts assist one another can they be fully perfected.
This refers to the remaining meaning of the previously discussed "perfect understanding.
Second, a specific inquiry regarding the hells.
“World-Honored One!

For instance, the bhikṣuṇī Ratnaprabhā, while upholding the Bodhisattva precepts, secretly engaged in sexual misconduct and falsely claimed that sexual conduct is neither killing nor stealing, and thus carries no karmic retribution.”
Having spoken these words, first a great, fierce fire arose from his female organ, and subsequently his body was consumed by flames joint by joint; he fell into the Avīci Hell.

As for King Virūḍhaka and the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—Virūḍhaka because he slaughtered the clan of the Gautamas, and Sunakṣatra because he falsely proclaimed that all dharmas are empty—they both sank alive into the Avīci Hell.
Do these various hells have fixed locations,
or do they arise spontaneously?
Do beings experience them individually according to the specific karma they have generated?

The source for the story of Ratnapadmagandha has not yet been verified; however, my view is that killing and stealing involve resistance (*sapratigha*), whereas sexual misconduct does not, which is why it was said there is no retribution.
The account of Sunakṣatra appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and the circumstances regarding Virūḍhaka are as found in the original sūtra.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether there is a fixed location, the underlying intent comprises six points, though the text manifests them in three.
These six are: having a fixed location and lacking a fixed location; spontaneity and causal conditions; individual reception and collective reception.
The subsequent text concludes: "Without severing the three karmas, each has its own private [attachments].
Because of these individual privacies, the collective share of these privacies has a fixed location; it is not without a definite place."
2. Request for Explanation and the Expression of Benefit:

"We beseech you to bestow great compassion and enlighten our ignorance, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear this definitive meaning, receive it with joy and veneration, and remain pure and unerring."
"Those who are young and small are called children; those whose minds are clouded are called the ignorant.
Ānanda deems himself base and lacking great wisdom, and thus prays that you will grant him instruction.
As for those who uphold the precepts, if they hear that cause and effect are as false as flowers in the sky, what benefit would there be in upholding the precepts?"
If one demonstrates the gateway to the definitive meaning, one must certainly cause others to be reverent, pure, and free from transgressions.
Second, the Tathāgata’s response has two parts:
first, praising the request and granting permission to proclaim it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"How excellent is this question!
It shall cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
That which is mundane is itself the true, being the single, wondrous awakening;
that which is true is itself the mundane, such that cause and effect are not lost.
Only when these two meanings are fused together can there be perfect realization.
Ānanda’s question was well-suited to the Buddha’s mind; thus, the Buddha praised it as "how excellent! and thereby eliminated his own [Ānanda’s] false views.
Second, the actual analysis has three parts:
I. Clarifying [the subject] in general by way of feelings (*vedanā*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*);
this has three parts. A-1. General opening into two divisions; this text has two parts. A-1-1.
Presentation and enumeration.
“Ānanda! All sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure; yet due to deluded vision, deluded habits arise, and because of this, they are divided into internal and external parts.”
All dharmas are fundamentally true and have never arisen; it is through the conceptualization of thought that one perceives the arising of all dharmas.

If one can depart from thought, one will see that sentient beings, mountains, rivers, and lands are originally enlightened Buddhas; therefore, it is said that they are truly and fundamentally pure and true.

Although this is the case for those who have returned to the source, those who have not yet returned each rely on their deluded views to create karma and undergo retribution; therefore, the text below states: "These sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of rebirth, failing to attain true purity for immeasurable kalpas, all because they follow along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct."
Reversing these three types [of conduct], one further gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
That which has a name belongs to the realm of ghosts; that which lacks a name pertains to the celestial realms.
As existence and non-existence oppose and incline toward one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
Therefore it is said: "Due to that false seeing, false habit-energies arise," and so forth.
Second, the actual explanation, in two parts:
first, the internal division concerning the subjective mind (*qing*). Second... [text continues]
First, the explanation of the characteristics: "Ānanda!

The internal constituent is within the category of sentient beings; because of various attachments and defilements, deluded sentiments are aroused. As these sentiments accumulate without ceasing, they are able to produce the water of craving."

The sentiment of passionate attachment is precisely the root of birth and death for sentient beings; it is called the "internal division" (*antarbhāga*), where "division" (*bhāga*) carries the sense of a cause.
Because this emotional attachment sinks downward and can moisten karma to bring about rebirth, it is like water.
The external arises from internal resonance; thus, there is a water-circle pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
"Therefore, when sentient beings think of delicacies in their minds, water flows from their mouths.
When they think of others—whether with pity or resentment—tears fill their eyes."
"When greedily seeking wealth and treasures, the mind produces a flow of affection, and the entire body becomes lustrous and moist.
When the mind is attached and one engages in sexual misconduct, the two organs of male and female naturally discharge fluids.
This is an illustration drawn from empirical evidence.
Recollection (*smṛti*) is precisely mindfulness (*manasikāra*), having clear retention as its essential nature.
Since mindfulness involves both aversion and affection, it is divided into compassion and resentment.
Aversion arises from affection; thus, it does not transcend the defilement of emotional attachment.
Because the internal defilements of sentient beings manifest externally as such phenomena, they all flow like water.
Second, the conclusion: "Ānanda!..."
"Although various cravings differ, their flow and fetters are the same; moistened by them, one does not ascend but naturally falls downward—this is called the 'internal constituent.
Although the objects of craving differ, the mind that craves is one; therefore, it is said that their flow and fetters are the same."
"Outflow" (*āsrava*) means sinking downward; "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) means being bound and attached.
Since the cause does not ascend, the fruit likewise falls into ruin.
Second, regarding external factors in terms of perception (*saṃjñā*), there are two parts:
First, the explanation of the characteristics: “Ānanda!

The external realm is precisely that which lies outside the sphere of sentient beings. Because of their various yearnings and aspirations, they give rise to false conceptions; as these conceptions accumulate without ceasing, they are able to produce a superior vital energy.”
The fundamental cause of sentient beings' birth and death lies in their emotions; by becoming emotionally attached to defiled objects, they consequently fall.

Now, taking pure objects as the desired destination depends solely on one's mental conception rather than on emotion; this is therefore something beyond the ordinary realm of sentient beings, which is why it is called "extraordinary" (wàifēn).
"Qi" refers to the complexion of the vital energy.
"Therefore, when sentient beings maintain the prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure.
When they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their glances become heroic and resolute."
When the mind desires to be born in heaven, one dreams of soaring through the air.
When the mind dwells upon the Buddha-lands, sacred realms manifest in the darkness.
When attending upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one regards one’s own body and life as insignificant.
This is an illustration through cited examples.

A light and pure body, a majestic and courageous bearing, dreams of flying aloft, the manifestation of sacred realms, and a disregard for one's own life—these five are all sublime signs that arise from mental visualization.
"Yi" means resolute and courageous.
Second, the conclusion: "Ānanda!..."
"Although various perceptions differ, their lightness and buoyancy are the same; they soar and move without sinking, naturally transcending [the mundane]. This is called the 'external factor.
One rejoices in these external superior realms without being defiled by emotional attachments."
When thought becomes light and pure, it naturally moves with flight; this is the retribution of transcendence.
The above provides a general and brief explanation, yet has not yet distinguished between good and evil in detail.
2. A detailed analysis of the destinies and births, in two parts:
1. A general explanation of the karmic conditions of favorable and unfavorable progress. "Ānanda!..."

The continuous succession of birth and death throughout all worlds proceeds from habitual tendencies during life and flows through transformation at death. At the moment of passing away, before body heat and sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of one’s entire life manifest simultaneously; the death-process is regressive while the birth-process is progressive, as these two habitual tendencies intersect.
There are two aspects to "conformity" and "opposition":

first, regarding emotional disposition. All sentient beings love life and hate death; thus, life conforms to their disposition while death opposes it. Therefore, it is said that "life follows the flow of conformity, while death follows the current of transformation. Here, "transformation" (bian) is synonymous with "opposition" (ni).
Furthermore, at the time of entering the womb, all three conditions must be favorable for birth to occur; in death, this is not the case. Second, in terms of karma:
karma is capable of inducing results. Birth is a "favorable induction" (*ānulomika*), as it proceeds from cause to result; thus it is called "favorable habituation. Death is the opposite of this;
since there is no sense of growth or production, it is called "transformative flux" (*parivṛtti*).

At the junction of birth and death, before wind and fire have dispersed, the karmic causes and conditions of one’s lifelong conduct—both good and evil—all manifest at once; that which is strongest first leads the way, and one is immediately drawn toward the place of rebirth.
2. A Detailed Explanation of the Rising and Sinking of Sentiment and Thought, in five parts:
First, explaining pure thought.
"Those with dull thoughts will immediately fly upward and will certainly be born in the heavens."

If within the flying mind one simultaneously possesses merit, wisdom, and pure vows, the mind will naturally open and one shall behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, being reborn in all pure lands according to one’s vows.
There are two categories of these:

if one possesses only the perception [of the Pure Land] without concurrently cultivating merit and wisdom, then by merely upholding the precepts and detesting this body, one will certainly be reborn in the heavens;
if, while upholding the precepts, one also cultivates merit and wisdom and makes a vow to see the Buddha, deeply detesting the three realms, one will certainly be reborn in a Pure Land.

Upon seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions, one immediately attains the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); thus it is said that "the mind is opened," as described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
Second, when emotion is slight and thought is predominant:

"When emotion is slight and thought is predominant, one rises lightly but not far; one becomes an immortal who flies, a powerful ghost-king, a flying yakṣa, or a land-walking rākṣasa, roaming through the four heavens with unimpeded movement wherever one goes."
Because their conceptualizations are manifold, they possess mastery over flight; because their mental states are deficient, they assume the forms of seers or ghosts.

Beings of this class mostly rely on perverse conceptualizations and do not practice correctly; thus, they do not cultivate ethical discipline or wisdom, but merely cultivate perverted meditative concentration.
Because they do not maintain the precepts, they fall into the realm of ghosts and spirits; because they have cultivated meditative concentration, they possess great supernormal powers.
The causes for these distinctions are as explained above: it is still a case where conceptualization is predominant and wisdom is slight.
Among these, the four categories of immortals, ghosts, and so forth, may be assigned respectively to the numbers nine, eight, seven, and six.
If one's worldly passions predominate, they will certainly lack both precepts and meditative concentration, and will consequently fall into the three miserable realms.

"If among them there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma—whether by protecting the prohibitive precepts in accordance with those who observe them, or by protecting divine mantras in accordance with those who recite them, or by protecting meditative concentration and sustaining the patience of the Dharma—these individuals dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata."
This visualization, though occurring amidst many [distractions], still incorporates virtuous vows.

Although one may not maintain the precepts, if one possesses the vow of meditative concentration and upholds the dharanis of the precepts and dhyāna, this arises from past habituation; thus, even if one has violated the prohibitions, by recognizing one's transgressions, one generates a vow. This is one who is "swift in the vehicle but lax in the precepts," and is therefore able to perceive the Buddha within the bodies of the eight classes of beings.
Third, when feeling and thought are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans.
When thought is clear, one is intelligent; when feeling is obscure, one is dull-witted.
One does not ascend to become a celestial immortal, nor does one fall into the three miserable realms, remaining instead within the state of equality.
If one's conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is somewhat strong, the faculties will necessarily be sharp and intelligent;
if one's emotional attachment (*vedanā*) is somewhat heavy, the faculties will necessarily be dull and obtuse.
Although they are of the same human species, these differences also arise from their emotions and perceptions;
this is what is meant by "distinct retribution. Fourth:
"When emotion is predominant and thought is slight, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth—becoming heavy as the fur-bearing beasts or light as the winged fowl."
According to the subsequent text, this refers to the six *kāya* (senses) and four *saṃjñā* (perceptions).
"Born crosswise" (*hengsheng*) means born as lateral animals (*pangsheng*).
However, there are degrees of gravity: if the [karmic] emotions are somewhat heavy, one is retributively born as a running beast; hence they are called the "furry multitude" (*maoqun*).
If one desires to be somewhat stronger, one becomes a flying bird; thus they are called the feathered race (*pakṣigaṇa*).
To discuss their specific distinctions in detail is as explained in the section on "Birth by Category" and below.
"The seven emotions and three perceptions sink down into the water-circle and are born at the boundary of fire."
Receiving the fierce heat of fire, their bodies become those of hungry ghosts (*preta*), constantly being scorched.
Water can harm them; for hundreds of thousands of kalpas they have neither food nor drink.

"The limit of fire" (*tejodhātu-paryanta*) is the dwelling place of hungry ghosts; it extends downward from the water wheel (*abdhātu*) to the limit of the fire wheel (*tejo-dhātu*), close to the hells.

Regarding those who receive the air of fierce fire: due to the power of their karma, they receive the air of fierce fire as their body; therefore, they are constantly burned, with flames erupting from every joint. Regarding those for whom water can harm them:
they suffer from the lack of water, and if they happen to encounter fire, it burns their bodies; hence it is said that [water] harms them.

"With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of goodness, they descend through the wheel of fire; their bodies enter the ground where wind and fire intersect, giving rise to two kinds of hells: the Intermittent Hell for those with lighter karma, and the Uninterrupted Hell for those with heavier karma."
Regarding the second, the ground of intersecting calamities: this refers to the junction between the two wheels of wind and fire, which is precisely the location of the seven hot hells.
Among the nine afflictions, those that are slightly diminished are termed "light"; thus, those with eight afflictions fall into the *sāntara* (intermittent) hells.
That which increases slightly is called "heavy" (guru), entering the ninth stage of the Uninterrupted (*avīci*) hell.
This term "uninterrupted" is spoken in reference to the experience of suffering.
Nevertheless, this "uninterrupted" receives its name in contrast to the preceding [hells] which have intervals, as it is the seventh hot hell.
Below is the eighth, the Five Uninterrupted Hells (*pañcānantarya-naraka*), specifically named Avīci, which is the most extreme and heavy.
Fifth, those of pure emotion:
"Those of pure emotion sink into the Avīci Hell."

If one harbors malice in the heart, slanders the Mahāyāna, violates the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, speaks deceptive and false teachings, vainly covets offerings of faith, unworthily receives respect and honor, or commits the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses, they will further be reborn in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions.
"Avīci," which is translated here as "Uninterrupted," is the eighth hell. It possesses five characteristics:
namely, the nature of the retribution, the instruments of suffering, the physical dimensions of the body, the number of kalpas, and the lifespan.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, karmic retribution is immediate because one who commits such a transgression will necessarily fall into hell, as no other karma or other birth can intervene.
Slandering the Mahāyāna is the most grievous of all sins; because of this, one is reborn in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If one slanders this sūtra, at the end of that person's life they shall enter the Avīci Hell for the full duration of one kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again, continuing in this manner through countless kalpas."
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that "the lifespan in the Avīci Hell is one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Twenty cycles of increase and decrease constitute one intermediate kalpa.
Since it is said to be "innumerable," when this world-system perishes, [beings] immediately go to the Avīci hells of the ten directions.
Because the sin of slandering the Dharma cuts off the lineage of the Buddhas and causes immeasurable people to fall into false views.
Third, the conclusion concerns one's own karma:
"While one invites [retribution] for oneself by following the commission of evil karma, within the commonality of beings (nikāya-sabhāga), there is also the fundamental ground."
Because one follows along with the commission of evil, one consequently undergoes the retribution of suffering.
Since the various types of evil karma differ, the retributions received are also distinct; therefore, it is said that one "invokes it for oneself.

Regarding the phrase "within the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) there is the original ground": the term *nikāya* has many names, yet they share the same essential meaning. Because there is a similarity among the members of a group, the name *sabhāga* (common portion) is established. Those who have performed identical karma undergo a collective transformation within that commonality.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "There are specific homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) and non-specific homogeneity.
When many beings, through common karma, experience a multitude of instruments of suffering and undergo that same suffering together, it is called non-specific homogeneity.
If one receives different retributions according to the gravity or lightness [of karma], it is called "differentiation within the homogeneous class" (bhinnā sabhāgatā).
What is now termed the "original ground" (mūlabhūmi) refers precisely to this differentiation.
Second, distinguishing [the realms] specifically by means of karmic retribution, there are seven [points]:
First, regarding the hells, there are three parts:
first, connecting the preceding section to the subsequent one: "Ānanda!..."
"All these are what those sentient beings have been moved to by their own karma; they created the ten habitual causes and receive the six intersecting retributions.

Because various karmas are falsely accumulated through emotional attachments and perceptions, one ascends or falls according to whether the karma is good or evil; therefore, it is said that "they are moved to by their own karma."

The ten habitual causes specifically refer to unwholesome karma; that is, by means of the ten underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*), consciousness is produced at the gates of the six sense organs, whereby karma is created and its retribution subsequently experienced.
Emerging from the six sense organs, retribution and karma intersect; hence it is called "intersecting retribution.

That they collectively undergo the hells is what is summoned by leading karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); that they individually undergo [sufferings] through the six organs is brought about by completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*). Both are merely the products of the habitual delusions of sentient beings.
II. Detailed Analysis of the Enumeration: Two parts.
A. The Ten Habitual Causes: One, the habit of sexual desire.
“What are the ten causes?
This is a general inquiry.
There are two ways in which karma is initiated:
The first is the primary initiator, which is ignorance;
the second is the auxiliary initiator, which consists of the other afflictions along with their associated conceptualizations.

Of these ten causes, the habit of sexual desire is the karma that is initiated, while the remaining nine are all the afflictions that initiate it. These afflictions comprise both the root and the derivative, as will be pointed out in the following text.
Each of the following ten sections contains three parts. "Ānanda!
First, as for the habit of lustful practice: it arises from mutual friction; through this ceaseless rubbing and grinding, a great and fierce fire is thereby ignited within."
"It is like a person rubbing their hands together; the sensation of warmth appears before them.
First, results are brought about by causes.
This is precisely the karma that is produced, which is fully possessed of greed and delusion, and serves as the very foundation for the cycle of birth and death.
The internal faculties and external objects mutually couple with one another; hence they are said to "interact.
As the internal and external stimulate each other, the fire of desire is thereby produced, which can be understood through this metaphor.
"Because the two habits ignite one another, there are such things as the iron bed and the copper pillar."
2. The characteristics of the actualization of the fruit:
Because both faculties and objects are present, they are called the "two habits.

The subject that touches and the object that is touched are both my own mind, which mutually perfumes one another to form the karma of lust; this occurs because one gives rise to a perverted mind toward sensual objects, conceiving the notion of pleasure for oneself and others.

Due to these karmic seeds, one later experiences their retribution: from those [seeds] capable of contacting a hellish body, and from those contacted by various instruments of suffering, all are perfumed by one's own karma; thus, through the interaction of these two habitual tendencies, they mutually inflict harm upon one another.
All other cases are to be understood in this same manner.
"Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct with the same term, 'the fire of desire'; a Bodhisattva views desire as one would avoid a pit of fire."
3. Conclusion and Identification of the Fault:
Fire can destroy and corrupt all things in the world, whereas desire can destroy and annihilate the supramundane wholesome dharmas; therefore, the practitioner should remain far removed from it.
2. The Habitual Tendency of Greed.

"Second, the habitual tendency of greed involves mutual calculation, arising from mutual attraction; as this attraction and grasping do not cease, there consequently comes to be accumulated cold and solid ice within, freezing and chilling."
"Just as when a person draws in air through the mouth, a sensation of cold arises;
this is because a cause brings about its fruit.

Greed (*lobha*) is one of the categories of the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it is precisely that which moistens rebirth, having the nature of being stained by attachment toward existence (*bhava*) and the requisites of existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*).
Due to attachment, one engages in various calculations and seeks to grasp external objects; thus it is said that "they calculate together and attract one another.
When greedy grasping does not cease, it is like water freezing into ice, remaining firm and not dispersing, thereby forming the analogy of being frozen solid.
This explains how long-accumulated karma born of greed leads to its fruition.
The metaphorical text is clear.
"Because the two habits contend with one another, there arise the *ṭaṭa*, *papa*, and *arara* hells, as well as the blue, red, and white lotuses, and the Cold Ice [Hell], and so forth."
This clearly reveals the characteristics of the result.
Because causes produce results, the internal produces the external.
*Ta*, *pa*, *ra*, and so forth, are sounds of enduring cold; these refer to the eight cold hells.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Arbuda means 'blister' (*ni*);
nirarbuda means 'bursting blister. These two [names] are derived from their physical characteristics."
*Akṣaṭā*, *Hūhūvā*, and *Huhuvā*: these three derive from sound. *Utpala* and the other two:
like the blue, white, and red lotuses, these three derive from color.
Because the cold becomes increasingly severe, the color of one's body becomes like it.
"Mutual transgression" means mutual encroachment.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking by the same name as the "water of greed," and Bodhisattvas view greed as they would avoid a sea of miasma.
This concludes the explanation of the name of the fault.
Greed can moisten and cause unwholesome dharmas to grow, just as there is a spring today; to drink from it is greed.
Furthermore, it can damage the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom, like a sea infested with miasma.
Third, the habit of pride:

"Third, the habit of pride involves mutual aggression arising from mutual reliance; it flows and surges without ceasing. Because of this, there are surging and rushing movements, and the accumulation of these waves forms water."
Just as when a person’s mouth and tongue rub against each other, saliva is produced;
so too, through the mutual friction of these two habits, there arise the various phenomena of rivers of blood, rivers of ash, hot sands, seas of poison, and molten copper being poured and swallowed.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize pride as "drinking the water of delusion"; when Bodhisattvas encounter pride, they avoid it as they would a great drowning.
(The three sections are as before.)
To rely on oneself and oppress others, taking loftiness as one's nature, is therefore called pride (*māna*).
What is now described as mutual oppression, mutual reliance, galloping about, and dissipation, are the manifestations of pride.
Matters such as the river of blood are all retributions experienced; they arise from within and manifest externally, for cause and effect correspond to one another.
Because drinking it leads to delusion and confusion, it is called the "water of folly" (moha-udaka); this exists in the Western Regions.
The great drowning can be understood [from the preceding].
Fourth, the habit-energy of anger:

"Fourth, the habit-energy of anger involves mutual conflict; arising from mutual opposition, this opposition knots together without ceasing. The mind becomes feverish and ignites fire, forging the vital breath into metal. For this reason, there exist mountains of knives, iron stakes, sword-trees, sword-wheels, axes, halberds, spears, and saws."

Just as when a person harbors a grievance, a murderous aura surges forth; because these two habits strike one another, there arise various matters such as castration, dismemberment, decapitation, hacking, mincing, stabbing, and beating.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize anger as a sharp sword; Bodhisattvas view anger as they would avoid execution.

When one increases anger toward various instruments of suffering, heat and affliction dwell within the mind and body, and one’s nature becomes unstable—these aforementioned states are all subsumed under the root delusions.
Mutually clashing and colliding, they form intense affliction (*paritāpa*); as this affliction does not cease, the energy of their fury solidifies, thereby inducing objects such as metal and stone.
"Nailing" refers to the stake used for binding sinners.
Cutting off the nose was one of the five punishments of the Qin dynasty.
Beheading, hacking, and mincing were all newly established forms of capital punishment.
Branding was equivalent to the ancient punishment of tattooing; it exists today as a form of exile.
Beating and striking are both types of new punishments involving canes and staves.

As in the age of the end of the eon, when people give rise to fierce and sharp anger, even the grass and wood they grasp turn into swords and blades—is this not brought about by what is stirred within the mind?
Five, the habit of deceit:

"The fifth is the habit of deceitful enticement, arising from mutual banter and inciting others without ceasing; because of this, there are the punishments of binding with ropes and wood, and the stocks and manacles."
Just as when water irrigates a field, grasses and trees grow,
so too do these two habits perpetuate one another, resulting in such matters as cangues, shackles, stocks, fetters, whips, staves, clubs, and cudgels.

Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize the deceitful and the false as being identical to slanderers and thieves; when Bodhisattvas encounter fraud, they regard it with the same dread as they would a jackal or a wolf.
"Fraud" refers to sycophancy and crookedness, which involve deceiving and overreaching others.
They feign extraordinary deportment and take deviousness as their nature.

Whether by seizing upon the intentions of others or concealing their own faults, they fail to submit to the correct instruction and admonition of teachers and friends; this is the "conformity to numbers."
What is now called "arising from mutual conditioning" and "inducing instability" refers precisely to this.
Deceitful and treacherous in its many forms, it may even disrupt the virtuous.
By feigning expedient means, they entice one another; hence it is called "mutual inducement."
Ropes, wooden stocks, and the act of strangulation are the instruments of suffering experienced there.
When evil grows long and spreads like creeping vines, it is like water soaking a field.
The *śṛgāla* (jackal) has feet like those of a dog and walks in packs; its tongue possesses backward-pointing spines.
Fierce, with a sharp head, white cheeks, a large tail, and long whiskers; it resembles a dog.
Its deceit and hypocrisy subvert what is correct, just like slanderous thieves.
Sixth, the habit of deception.

"Sixth, the habit-energy of deception arises from mutual delusion; as this false deception does not cease, the mind soars toward the commission of wickedness. For this reason, there exist dust, soil, excrement, urine, and all manner of foul, impure filth."
Just as dust particles following the wind cannot see one another,
so too, through the mutual interaction of these two habits, there arise various phenomena such as sinking and drowning, leaping and tossing upward, flying and falling, and drifting and submerging.

Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions identify deception as being synonymous with murderous violence; when Bodhisattvas encounter deception, they view it as treading upon venomous snakes and vipers.
This, too, follows the enumeration.
Deceit (*māyā*) refers to hypocrisy and guile; it involves harboring ulterior motives and frequently manifesting what is unreal.
Its nature is to falsely display virtue and to employ craftiness and fraud; its function is to constitute a wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Now it is said that they "mutually deceive"; "deception" (qī) is synonymous with "fraud" (kuàng).
To "mislead and delude" is precisely to manifest the practices of wrong livelihood in order to entice profit and fame.
Dust, soil, excrement, and urine are all instruments of suffering.
During the kalpa of weapons (*śastra-kalpa*), people kill and harm one another; hence it is called "kalpa-slaughter.
As for the *huǐfù* (vipers), they are *huǐ* snakes, three inches in width with heads like a thumb.
Seventh, the habit-energy of resentment (*vaira-vāsanā*).

"Seventh, the habit-energy of resentment arises from harboring hatred; because of this, there are flying stones, projectiles, stone boxes, carriage-cages, jars, and bags—like a person of hidden malice who nurtures evil within their breast."
As these two habits devour one another, there arise various acts such as hurling, seizing, striking with projectiles, and grappling.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate an enemy as a "hostile and harmful ghost" (vi-hai-ghoṣa), and a Bodhisattva views an enemy as if drinking poisoned wine (viṣa-madya).
"Enmity" (*upanāha*) is resentment; having anger as its precursor, it consists in harboring malice without relinquishing it, taking the nature of binding a grudge.
Because one cannot endure [the offense] and is constantly tormented by heat.
The items such as bags and bundles listed above are all implements for binding and restraining criminals; there are instances where the character "pò" (to strike) is erroneously used.
"Wǎn" (to pull) and "cuō" (to seize) both refer to dragging and binding criminals; there are also instances where "pāo" (to throw) is used, which is likewise an error in the text.
It is like the *vighna* (obstructing) spirits who constantly lie in wait to seize people.
As for "poisoned wine" (*zhènjiǔ*): *zhèn* is the name of a bird; if its wing feathers are used to stir the wine, the wine will kill the person who drinks it.
Eighth, the perception of habitual tendencies (*dṛṣṭivāsanā*).

"Eighth, the habit-energy of views intermingles with clarity; such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the karmas of false awakening, which arise from opposition and produce mutually contradictory results. For this reason, there exist royal messengers, chief clerks, and those who examine and hold legal documents, like travelers on a road meeting one another as they pass back and forth."

As the two habitual tendencies intersect, there arise matters such as interrogation, guile, examination, cross-examination, investigation, scrutiny, illumination, and the various affairs involving good and evil youths who hold registers and exercise eloquence.

Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate evil views with the same term: "the pit of views. When Bodhisattvas encounter various delusions and grasp at them universally, it is as if they have entered a ravine of poison.

"View" refers to wrong view; its nature is defiled wisdom that erroneously speculates upon the principles of the truths, it functions as an obstacle to right view, and its activity is to bring about suffering.
There are five distinctions in the characteristics of these views:
first, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to a self and what belongs to a self;
second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which clings to annihilationism or eternalism.
Third is the false view of nihilism (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which slanders the existence of cause and effect;

fourth is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which refers to the attachment to various views and their underlying aggregates as being supreme and capable of attaining purification, having the function of serving as the basis for all conflict;

fifth is the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which refers to the attachment to precepts, observances, and their underlying aggregates that accord with those views as being supreme and capable of attaining purification, having the function of serving as the basis for fruitless toil and suffering.

These habitual tendencies of views cause each to cling to their own interpretations and contend with one another over right and wrong; thus, they bring about such matters as royal messengers and chief officials.
As for "deceit," it refers to employing expedient means to extract the truth [of others' intentions].
“Illumination” means to cite other matters as evidence for illumination.
Ninth, the habituation of calumny:

“Ninth, when the habituation of calumny intermingles, it issues forth in slander. Because of this, there are mountains joined together, rocks joined together, grinding mills, and plowing and treading; it is like a slanderous villain encountering the virtuous and good who have been wronged.”
As these two habits contend with one another, there arise various acts such as pressing down, striking, squeezing, and measuring across.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the act of slandering and calumniating by the same name, "the slanderous tiger," and when a Bodhisattva encounters such injustice, it is like being struck by a bolt of lightning.
"Persecution" refers to the oppression of the virtuous and the infliction of harm upon others, characterized by a lack of compassion; it is subsumed under the category of "harm.
Since one has unjustly oppressed the virtuous and suppressed the innocent, forcing them to be labeled as guilty, one consequently experiences such events as being buried under mountains.
"Ji" means oppression; "lu" means vibration.
"Heng" refers to the balance scale;
"du" refers to the measuring rod.
Slander can harm the virtuous, and tigers can devour humans.
Tenth is the habit of litigation.

This habit of litigation arises from the concealment of one's deeds within the mind; because of this, there is the mirror of discernment and the lamp of illumination. Just as one cannot hide a shadow in the midst of the sun, so too do the karmic mirror and the fire-jewel of evil companions reveal past karma, verifying all matters through direct confrontation.

Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate concealment with the same name: the "hidden thief. A Bodhisattva views concealment as if bearing a mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean.
This is *mrakṣa* (concealment); as for what is called "litigation," it is because litigation arises from concealment.
That which is called concealment has the nature of hiding one's own committed transgressions out of fear of losing profit and reputation, and its function is remorse and affliction.
This means that one who conceals their transgressions will inevitably experience remorse and distress later on, as they lack peace and security.
Having committed a fault oneself, being unable to confess it, one subsequently invites litigation from others.

This litigation is itself a dharma of affliction; it is preceded by anger and resentment, characterized by a violent heat that pursues and strikes at the offender, having a nature of malice and hostility, and functioning to sting and bite like an insect.

This refers to when one recalls past evils and encounters adverse conditions in the present, causing the mind to become resentful and perverse; it then gives rise to much clamorous, violent, and wickedly vulgar speech, and because it stings and bites others, it is called "litigation" (sòng).
This concealment and that litigation mutually stimulate one another; thus, they bring about such matters as evil companions and the mirror of karma.

To conceal one's transgressions and evils, knowing only oneself, is like being unafraid of future suffering due to a hidden enemy; one will inevitably fall into the evil realms, as if carrying a mountain upon one's head while treading across the ocean.
